analysis.one_liner: Imposes a tiny tax on Wall Street trades of stocks, bonds, and derivatives.
analysis.headline: A bill to tax financial trades by 3 cents per $1,000 was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in 2013 and never received a vote, with only three senators signed on.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a 0.03% tax (30 cents per $1,000) on purchases of stocks, bonds, derivatives, and similar instruments traded in the U.S. or by U.S. parties. High-frequency trading firms and banks making thousands of rapid trades would pay the most. Contributions to retirement, health, and college savings accounts would get a matching credit so ordinary savers are not charged the tax. The revenue would go to the Treasury without being earmarked for any specific program.
analysis.who_benefits: The federal Treasury, which would collect revenue from financial firms and heavy traders. Ordinary retirement, health, and college savers are protected: contributions to tax-favored accounts earn a credit that refunds the tax on the trades those accounts generate. If the tax slows rapid-fire speculative trading, any benefit from steadier markets would also flow to ordinary investors.

how_it_helps.text: The bill taxes each purchase of a stock, bond, derivative, or similar instrument at 0.03% when the trade happens or clears on a U.S. trading facility or involves a U.S. party, so the tax falls on trading volume — the biggest cost falls on firms that trade constantly.
It exempts initial stock and bond offerings, so companies raising money for investment would not pay the tax.

It gives a credit equal to 0.03% of contributions to retirement plans, health savings accounts, medical savings accounts, and 529 and Coverdell college savings plans, so money ordinary families put into those accounts is effectively shielded from the tax.
It closes an easy escape route by treating controlled foreign corporations as U.S. persons, so a firm cannot dodge the tax by running trades through an overseas subsidiary it owns.

analysis.who_pays: Banks, hedge funds, and especially high-frequency trading firms would bear the direct cost, since the tax applies to every qualifying purchase including derivatives. Trading facilities like exchanges and brokers would be responsible for collecting and paying the tax, and some of that cost would likely be passed on to investors through slightly higher transaction costs.

drawbacks.text: Because brokers and trading facilities are made responsible for paying the tax, some of the cost would likely be passed through to all investors in the form of higher transaction costs or wider spreads, not just to Wall Street firms.
The bill does not dedicate its revenue to any specific program; it would simply add to general Treasury funds, so taxpayers would not be able to see a direct benefit in exchange for the new tax.

Opponents of transaction taxes generally argue they can reduce trading volume and could modestly lower investment returns for pension funds and mutual funds that hold ordinary people's savings, though the bill's credit for retirement account contributions is meant to offset part of that.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax is small enough that a family making a handful of trades a year would pay pennies, while heavy traders would pay real money; the credit for retirement and college accounts further shields ordinary savers. The honest objection is that the bill says nothing about what the money would fund, so voters were asked to accept a new tax on finance without a promised benefit, and pass-through costs would touch even small investors' accounts. On balance the design targets speculation while sparing new investment and ordinary savings accounts.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until that Congress ended two years later, with no hearing, no vote, and no action of any kind.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Harkin introduced the bill on February 28, 2013, joined by Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse and Bernie Sanders.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action was ever recorded; the bill never received a hearing or a vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial firms and heavy traders are better off, since no trading tax was ever enacted. Ordinary savers were spared the small pass-through costs the tax would have added to trades, but they also never received whatever public benefit the revenue might have funded.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to impose a 0.03% tax on financial trading transactions.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Max Baucus (D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only three senators backed the bill — two Democrats and one independent — and no vote ever occurred, so the partisan split was never tested; no Republican supported it at any stage.

industries.note: The tax applies to every qualifying purchase of stocks, bonds, and derivatives, including each leg of rapid-fire strategies, so firms trading at enormous volume would pay far more than occasional investors. Their gain from blocking the bill came at the cost of revenue that could have served the public.

Their large-scale trading and derivatives activity would have been taxed, including derivatives on currencies and commodities and notional principal contracts, with trades through foreign subsidiaries still covered.

industries.industry: Securities and derivatives exchanges and brokers
industries.note: Exchanges and brokers would carry the compliance job of collecting and remitting the tax, and if trading volume fell, so would their fee income.

industries.industry: Retirement, health, and college savings account holders
industries.note: Their account trades would technically be taxed, but a matching credit on contributions to 401(k)-type plans, HSAs, and 529 college accounts would refund that cost to them.
